title: MMI Teamwork Station: Conflict Over a Shared Project
prompt: You are one of four students assigned to a graded group presentation due in three days. One team member, Jordan, has missed the last two planning meetings and has not completed the section everyone agreed they would prepare. Two of your teammates are frustrated and want to report Jordan and exclude them from the credit. Jordan has just messaged the group saying they can meet tonight. How would you handle this situation?
blurb: A teamwork/conflict MMI station: resolving a group conflict fairly while protecting the shared goal.

rubric.label: Conflict resolution
rubric.description: Seeks to understand the cause before judging; de-escalates the frustrated teammates; aims for a constructive resolution rather than punishment; distinguishes the immediate task from the interpersonal issue.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: Proposes a direct, private, non-accusatory conversation with Jordan; uses open questions; communicates clearly with the wider group without taking sides prematurely.

rubric.label: Empathy
rubric.description: Considers that Jordan may have a legitimate reason (illness, personal crisis, misunderstanding of the task); treats them charitably while still addressing the problem.

rubric.label: Structure & problem-solving
rubric.description: Separates the urgent goal (finishing the presentation in 3 days) from the accountability question; makes a concrete plan; assigns/redistributes work realistically.

rubric.label: Fairness & accountability
rubric.description: Balances fairness to the teammates who did the work against giving Jordan a chance to contribute; avoids both a cover-up and an unfair exclusion; knows when escalation to a supervisor is warranted.

rubric.label: Leadership & initiative
rubric.description: Takes initiative to keep the group functioning without being domineering; brings people together toward the shared objective.

rubric.label: Professionalism
rubric.description: Keeps the matter within the group where possible, avoids gossip, models collegial behavior, and recognizes team dynamics as a core clinical skill.

reference.scenario: The candidate is part of a four-person graded group project. A teammate (Jordan) has been absent and has not delivered their agreed section three days before the deadline. Two teammates want to report and exclude Jordan. Jordan has just offered to meet tonight. The station tests conflict resolution, empathy, fairness, and the ability to keep a team focused on a shared goal under time pressure. There is no single right answer; the interviewer probes the trade-offs.
model_points: Separates two problems: the urgent shared goal (finish a good presentation in 3 days) and the interpersonal/accountability issue with Jordan.
Avoids rushing to judgment — seeks to understand why Jordan was absent before deciding on consequences (illness, family emergency, feeling excluded, misunderstanding).
De-escalates the two frustrated teammates: acknowledges their frustration is valid but steers away from immediate punitive action.
Takes up Jordan's offer to meet tonight; plans a private, calm, curious conversation rather than a group pile-on.
Uses open, non-accusatory questions ('We missed you at the meetings and we're worried — is everything okay? What happened with the section?').
Makes a concrete recovery plan: what Jordan can realistically deliver in 3 days, and how the group redistributes work if needed.
Balances fairness — the teammates who did the work deserve recognition, and Jordan should still be given a fair chance to contribute.
Identifies when escalation to a supervisor/course lead is appropriate (e.g., if Jordan disengages entirely or there's a safety/repeat pattern), and does so honestly rather than vindictively.
Models collegiality: keeps it within the team where possible, avoids gossip, focuses on the goal.
Frames teamwork and conflict management as a core clinical competency, not just an academic annoyance.

probes.trigger: candidate immediately sides with reporting/excluding Jordan
probes.question: Before you decide, is there anything you'd want to know first? What might explain Jordan's absence?

probes.trigger: candidate is overly lenient and ignores the frustrated teammates
probes.question: Your two teammates say they've done Jordan's share already and it isn't fair. How do you respond to them?

probes.trigger: candidate offers only a conversation with no plan for the deadline
probes.question: It's three days out. Concretely, how does the presentation actually get finished?
Suppose Jordan doesn't show up tonight either. Is there a point where you involve the supervisor, and how would you do it fairly?

probes.trigger: candidate proposes confronting Jordan in front of the whole group
probes.question: How do you think Jordan would respond to that, and is there a better setting for the conversation?

red_flags: Immediately agreeing to report and exclude Jordan without seeking any explanation.
Publicly confronting or shaming Jordan in the group chat or in front of others.
Ignoring the legitimate frustration of the teammates who did the work.
Avoiding the conflict entirely and hoping it resolves itself, jeopardizing the deadline.
Covering for Jordan dishonestly (e.g., claiming they contributed when they didn't) to keep the peace.
Taking a domineering, unilateral approach that overrides the team.
Treating the situation as purely academic with no reflection on teamwork as a clinical skill.
follow_ups: How would you open the conversation with Jordan tonight?
What would you say to the two frustrated teammates before that meeting?
How do you decide how to redistribute the work with only three days left?
At what point, if any, would you involve a supervisor, and how would you keep that fair to Jordan?
How does handling this well relate to working in a clinical team later?
reference.exemplar_answer: I'd treat this as two linked but separate problems: getting a good presentation done in three days, and understanding what's going on with Jordan. First I'd calm the two frustrated teammates — their frustration is fair, they've carried extra load — but I'd suggest we not report or exclude anyone before we understand why Jordan has been absent, because there could be a real reason like illness or a personal crisis, or they may have felt lost about the task. Jordan has offered to meet tonight, so I'd take that up and have a private, non-accusatory conversation: tell them we missed them, that we're a bit stuck, and ask openly what's been happening and what they can realistically contribute now. Then I'd make a concrete plan — if Jordan can deliver their section in the next two days, great; if not, we agree how to redistribute so the presentation is solid, and Jordan takes on something achievable so they're genuinely contributing. I'd want the outcome to be fair both ways: the people who did the extra work should be recognized, and Jordan gets a real chance rather than being written off. If Jordan simply disengaged, didn't show tonight, and left us carrying everything, then involving the course supervisor would be appropriate — but honestly and factually, not as punishment. Ultimately how a team handles this kind of friction is exactly the skill we'll need on a clinical team, so I'd want us to come out of it still working together.

interviewer_notes: Entry-level MMI teamwork/conflict station. Ask the candidate how they'd handle it and let them lead. Watch whether they instinctively seek Jordan's side before judging, and whether they can also validate the frustrated teammates — the best answers hold both. If they lean punitive, use the 'what would you want to know first' probe; if they're conflict-avoidant or too lenient, use the fairness probe from the teammates' side. Always push once for a concrete plan given the 3-day deadline — vague 'we'll talk it out' answers should be pressed for specifics. Escalation is acceptable when justified and handled fairly; reflexive reporting or total avoidance are both weak. No specific policy knowledge is required.
